nothingMatches: Nothing matches. {n} session(s) are live under other names or other protocols.
nothingSignedIn: Nothing is signed in. Sign somebody in — an OIDC flow, a SAML 2.0 sign-in, an ldapsearch that binds, a kinit — and a row appears here.
leadBefore: Every session this service is holding right now, across the three protocols that have one. A session is state THIS SERVICE holds that makes somebody currently authenticated; a token, an assertion, a ticket and an SVID are things it has HANDED OUT, they outlive every session here, and they are
leadAfter: . Keeping the two apart is the whole point of a page of each.
threeKinds: The three are not variants of one thing and their expiries are worked out differently, which is why the Expires column carries the rule as well as the time — hover it on any row:
kindBrowser: The browser sign-on session — the cookie from /authn/login, which OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, WS-Federation, SAML 2.0, SAML 1.1 and this console all read. It expires at an ABSOLUTE instant fixed when it was created (authn.sessionLifetimeS) and using it does not extend it. An idle timeout (authn.sessionIdleTimeoutS) ends it earlier when it goes unused; it is off by default, and then a session in constant use dies at the same moment as one nobody has touched. The Carries column is what has signed in ON it, which is what makes ending one reach further than it looks.
kindKerberos: The Kerberos ticket-granting ticket — a TGT IS the Kerberos session and a service ticket is one use of it. It expires at the endtime the KDC sealed INTO the ticket, and nothing here can move it or take it back: a ticket is valid because it decrypts and its endtime has not passed. Short lifetimes are the whole of Kerberos's revocation model.
kindLdap: The LDAP connection — RFC 4511 section 4.2 makes a Bind the authorization state of a CONNECTION, so in LDAP the connection is the session and closing it is the only sign-out the protocol has. It has no expiry at all: it lasts until the next Bind, an Unbind, or the socket closing.
revokeBefore: Revoke is not one act either. On a browser session it ends that session and everything hanging off it — the relying parties are notified, the refresh tokens issued on it are revoked. On an LDAP row it closes the socket, which the client sees as its connection dropping mid-conversation. On a Kerberos row it does more than the row it is on: it stamps a sign-out instant on the PRINCIPAL, so every ticket-granting ticket that principal authenticated before now is refused — and it still reaches no service ticket already in a cache, because accepting one never contacts this KDC. Every button carries its own sentence; hover it before pressing it. All three go through the same termination
revokeAfter: performs, so they write the same audit row and honour the same two settings.
searchPlaceholder: a username, a subject, a DN or a session id
searchNote: The search matches the username, the subject, the session id, the bind DN and the principal name together, because a reader arrives holding exactly one of those. The protocol is the one the sign-in came THROUGH and not the only one the session serves: every browser family here reads the same session, so a row saying SAML 2.0 may well be carrying OIDC relying parties too — which is what the Carries column says.
rowsOnPage: , of which rows {first}–{last} are on this page ({page} of {pages})
liveInTotal: ; {held} live in total. Newest first. Everything here is read live from the module that owns it every time this page is drawn — there is no cache, deliberately, because a cached answer to is this still live would be the half a reader is about to press a button on.
unauthLead: A session where nobody authenticated. Somebody pressed Continue without signing in at /authn/login, so this service holds a real session for them — it has a cookie, it satisfies a flow already in progress, and tokens can be issued on it — and it records that no credential was ever checked. They are the anonymous principal, which is one directory entry however many of these there are.
rolesBefore: This is the only place the difference between two of the built-in roles is visible. Every session in the table above holds EVERYBODY and ALL_AUTHENTICATED_USERS; every session in this one holds EVERYBODY and ALL_UNAUTHENTICATED_USERS instead. So an application whose appRequiredRole is ALL_AUTHENTICATED_USERS refuses these with access_denied, and one that names no role at all — which requires EVERYBODY — does not.
onBefore: authn.unauthenticatedSessions is ON in this realm, so the sign-in screen is offering the third button.
onAfter: and no new ones can be started; any already here stay until they expire or are ended.
offBefore: authn.unauthenticatedSessions is OFF in this realm, so no new ones can be started and this section will stay empty. It is off by default because it puts a third button on every sign-in screen in the service.
unauthCount: {n} unauthenticated session(s), of {held} live. Not filtered and not paged, unlike the table above — the question this section answers is about the whole service, and a search box somebody had left set could hide the one row that matters.
unauthNone: None. Every session this service is holding right now had a credential accepted for it.
